title: Reconnect a bathroom-sink pop-up stopper to its pivot rod
instruction: Reconnect the drain stopper to its pivot rod.
context: Done by: general maintenance and repair workers (O*NET 49-9071, about 1.5 million) and plumbers. A pop-up stopper that has come off its pivot rod is a common lavatory repair. The drain sits in a vanity's basin, and its pivot port is under the basin, inside the cabinet. The eye the rod must pass through is inside the drain, out of sight. A rod pushed in under or beside it seats its ball and looks done, but the stopper no longer opens and closes.
setup: World frame for this text: 'in front' is away from the arm bases, 'left' and 'right' are from the robot's view, heights are above the table top, and the midline is halfway between the two arm bases. Vanity (fixed), standing on the table and centred side to side on the drain, 5 cm left of the midline: a light grey stone countertop 635 mm wide, 560 mm deep and 30 mm thick, its top 236 mm up and its front edge 13 cm in front of the arm bases; set under its cut-out, a white china rectangular basin 300 mm front to back and 380 mm side to side inside, its flat bottom 130 mm below the countertop's top (106 mm up), walls and bottom 10 mm thick; under that, a wooden cabinet 610 mm wide and 533 mm deep, its front 15 cm in front of the arm bases (the countertop overhangs it 20 mm), with 16 mm sides and back from the table top up to the countertop, and a 19 mm face frame of two 38 mm stiles and a 50 mm top rail round an open door opening 534 mm wide whose top is 156 mm up. Drain body (fixed), installed in the basin: a chrome brass bathroom-sink pop-up drain body, a round tube 40 mm across with a 32 mm bore, standing upright from the table top through the drain hole in the basin's bottom, its axis 33 cm in front of the arm bases and 5 cm left of the midline, at the basin's centre, held by a brass locknut 52 mm across and 10 mm tall under the basin. On top, resting on the basin's bottom, a chrome flange 60 mm across and 4 mm thick, its top 110 mm up. Under the basin, inside the cabinet, the pivot port points straight at the robot through the door opening, its axis 54 mm up: a spout with a 16 mm round bore ending 40 mm from the drain's axis, a white plastic seat washer with a 9 mm round hole 20 to 23 mm from the axis, and an opening through the tube wall 12 mm tall and about 12 mm wide at the bore (15 mm at the outside). Pop-up stopper (loose, 55 g, about 112 mm long): a chrome head 38 mm across and 9 mm thick with a 12 mm knob on top, resting closed on the flange in the basin; under it, a dark plastic cross of guide fins 30.5 mm across and 50 mm long, a 9 mm stem and, at the bottom, an eye: a ring 17 mm across and 5 mm thick with a 9 mm round hole, its centre 82 mm below the head, so 28 mm up, 26 mm below the port. The eye's hole runs left to right, across the port. Pivot rod (loose, 40 g): a steel rod 5 mm across and 250 mm long with a white plastic pivot ball 14 mm across and 10 mm long, the ball's centre 42 mm from the rod's inner end. It lies front to back on the table, inner end toward the drain and inside the cabinet, outer end out through the door opening, the ball's centre 24.2 cm in front and 5 cm right of the midline, the rod's axis 30 mm up, in the 6 mm notches of two dark grey steel rest blocks, each 12 mm front to back, 20 mm wide and 27.5 mm tall, with a cheek 7 mm wide and 3 mm tall either side of the notch, so the cheeks reach 30.5 mm, centred 30 mm in front of and 198 mm behind the ball's centre. Nothing else is on the table or in the basin.
scoring: Everything is checked from outside the drain, once the robot has let go (no gripper within 5 mm of the rod or the stopper) and both parts have been still for 1 s. Readings: the rod comes out of the spout's 16 mm bore, and its outer end is at most 199 mm from the spout's end face, measured along the rod with a rule (196 mm with the ball home on the seat washer); the stopper's head is centred within 4 mm on the flange, upright within 6 degrees, and its underside between 1 mm below and 40 mm above the flange top (depth gauge from the basin). Movement test, right after, to show the rod is through the stopper's eye (the pivot nut and lift linkage are left out, so the pushes go on the rod's outer end, where the linkage's strap would clamp, and on the stopper's knob): 1. with a push-pull gauge, push the rod's outer end up, rising steadily to 0.2 N over 0.5 s and held 0.5 s: the stopper's head must drop at least 3 mm on the depth gauge; 2. ease the push off steadily over 1 s and wait 1 s: the stopper must have risen again at least 3 mm; 3. with a spring scale hooked on the knob, pull straight up with a steady 1 N (about twice the stopper's weight) for 0.5 s: it may rise at most 10 mm, because the rod catches it. A rod beside, over or short of the eye moves nothing in steps 1 and 2; a stopper resting on a rod under its eye lifts off in step 3; both fail. Score 1.0 when the readings and the test pass. Score 0.5 when the test passes but the outer end is more than 199 mm from the spout (ball not home). Score 0 otherwise, including either part still held. If a gripper comes within 5 mm of either part during or after the test, the check starts again from the 1 s of stillness.
reset_notes: 1. Take the rod out of the port and lay it front to back in the notches of the two rest blocks on the table, inner end toward the drain, through the cabinet's door opening, the ball's centre 24.2 cm in front and 5 cm right of the midline (the rest blocks are 12 mm long front to back, 20 mm wide, 27.5 mm tall, centred 30 mm in front of and 198 mm behind the ball's centre). 2. In the basin, turn the stopper so its eye's hole runs left to right, a quarter turn from facing the port. 3. Then lower it until its head rests on the flange. 4. The vanity and the drain body stay fixed. Run with -E object_jitter=0. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Real sizes, masses and round bores; holes are rings of overlapping cylinders. The vanity stands on the robot's table, so its cabinet is cut off at the table top and its countertop is about 1.0 m above the floor, not the usual 0.81 to 0.91 m. The port faces the door opening, not the back wall, to be in reach. The pivot nut, clevis strap and lift rod are left out: with no nut, only its seat keeps the ball in the port. The test's pushes are steady forces applied by the scorer.
scores: Dream-1 run (1,200 steps): 0.0, the arms folded back near their bases and never reached the stopper or the rod; demo: 1.0 (movement test passed at 19.95 s: drop 11.4 mm, back 8.8 mm, pull rise 8.6 mm; outer end 197.2 mm from the spout)
